messages.subject: Analysis Help - Trial Outcomes
parts:
Hey D-RUG,

I'm working on a side project that is analyzing the outcomes of a reality show. Competitors sing against each other one-on-one in a 'battle' and there is one winner and one loser.

I have a data set with various characteristics of the performances (e.g. "high energy performance", "does splits"). Most of the variables are binary with a couple of integers (e.g. "number of acrobatic tricks"). I've already done logistic regression to identify absolute characteristics of winners and losers, but now I want to look at how various factors interact within the battles themselves (for example, just looking at the data suggests "high energy" tends to win when competing against "low energy").

What's the right method to go about looking for these interactions?

csv is attached just in case it's useful.

--
Thanks,
Erica


Erica Rettig
PhD Candidate

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Analysis Help - Trial Outcomes
parts:
Hi Erica,

Interesting problem!

Caveat: I don't have deep experience this type of data, but here's what I'm :

1a. construct a vector of the difference between winner and loser for each variable to make new 'winner - loser' predictors (looking at the data, it seems some of the columns should be aggregated to one new predictor as they describe different levels of the same trait)
1b. choose a difference metric to construct each of these new predictors
2. code a new variable as "success"
3a. predict success using logistic regression based on all combinations of the new predictors
3b. there are ~ 60 battles so unless the current variables aggregate to < 3-4 new predictors, with all interactions, you're looking at too many potential predictors for standard regressions. If that's the case, you'd need regularized or Bayesian glm (maybe packages glmnet or blme would help)
4. ideally, expand the model to accommodate the hierarchical structure in the data (repeated trails of some contestants within and seasons)
5. estimated parameter for the new predictors then inform relative importance of differences in determining the winner

Good luck,
